\chapter{Mother, Father, Brother, Daughter}
\label{ch:fa-family}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my mother, father, brother, and daughter in Persian, the four secure English cousins Chapter 6 named without teaching.}

The chapter closes on dokhtar, daughter, then runs all four family words back to back and reuses the ezafe from esm-e man ast and kelid-e man to say dokhtar-e man, my daughter.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mâdar]{\fa{مادر} — mother, a word this track already promised you}

\label{lesson:FA-C10-madar}



\begin{quote}
The \textbf{\fa{بودن}} lesson traced it back to English \textbf{be}, and in passing named four plainest inherited cousins the track had not yet taught as their own lessons: \textbf{\fa{مادر}}, \textbf{\fa{پدر}}, \textbf{\fa{برادر}}, \textbf{\fa{دختر}}. This chapter and the next finally give each one its own lesson, starting here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{مادر}} — \emph{mâdar} — \textbf{mother}
\end{quote}

Four letters, all already yours: \textbf{\fa{م} \fa{ا} \fa{د} \fa{ر}} — \emph{m}, long \emph{â}, \emph{d}, \emph{r}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{مادر}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{mādar}, from Indo-European *\emph{méh\textsubscript{2}tēr} — the same root English wore down to \textbf{mother}, German to \emph{Mutter}, Latin to \emph{māter} (giving English \textbf{maternal}), and Sanskrit to \textbf{mātṛ}. Few words in any language family stay this recognisable after four thousand years; a mother is called almost the same thing across most of Eurasia because small children the world over reach for the same easy sounds.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mâdar} — mother
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{mâdar} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{méh\textsubscript{2}tēr} $\to$ English \textbf{mother}, Latin \textbf{māter}, Sanskrit \textbf{mātṛ}
  \item \emph{Retrieve:} \textbf{kelid-e man, lotfan} — my key, please
  \item \emph{Name:} which four family words the \textbf{\fa{بودن}} lesson promised, and which one this lesson delivers
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\fa{مادر}} mean? (\textbf{Mother.}) Which lesson first named it as an English cousin, without teaching it as its own word? (\textbf{The \fa{بودن} lesson}, in passing.) Which three family words does the track still owe you? (\textbf{\fa{پدر}}, \textbf{\fa{برادر}}, \textbf{\fa{دختر}}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%85\%D8\%A7\%D8\%AF\%D8\%B1}{Wiktionary: \fa{مادر}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pedar]{\fa{پدر} — father, mâdar's oldest partner}

\label{lesson:FA-C10-pedar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\fa{مادر}}, and its English cousin. This lesson's word has kept the same partnership for four thousand years.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{پدر}} — \emph{pedar} — \textbf{father}
\end{quote}

Three letters, all already yours: \textbf{\fa{پ}} \emph{p}, from \textbf{\fa{پرسیدن}}; \textbf{\fa{د}} \emph{d}; \textbf{\fa{ر}} \emph{r}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{پدر}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{pidar}, from Indo-European *\emph{ph\textsubscript{2}t\'{\={e}}r} — the direct cousin of English \textbf{father}, German \emph{Vater}, and Latin \emph{pater} (giving English \textbf{paternal}, \textbf{patriot}). \textbf{\fa{مادر}} and \textbf{\fa{پدر}} are not just similar in meaning; they are built the same way, both old Indo-European kinship words carrying a shared \textbf{-ar/-tar} ending that once meant something close to “the one who {[}does the kin role{]}.”
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{pedar} — father
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{pedar} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{ph\textsubscript{2}t\'{\={e}}r} $\to$ English \textbf{father}, Latin \textbf{pater}
  \item \emph{Pair:} \textbf{mâdar} — \textbf{pedar}, both carrying the same old kinship ending
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{mâdar, pedar} — mother, father
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\fa{پدر}} mean? (\textbf{Father.}) Which English word is it the direct cousin of? (\textbf{Father}, via \textbf{pater}.) What ending do \textbf{\fa{مادر}} and \textbf{\fa{پدر}} share? (An old kinship ending, \textbf{-ar/-tar}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%BE\%D8\%AF\%D8\%B1}{Wiktionary: \fa{پدر}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[barâdar]{\fa{برادر} — brother, the cousin that never drifted}

\label{lesson:FA-C10-baradar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\fa{مادر}} and \textbf{\fa{پدر}}. One family word from the \textbf{\fa{بودن}} lesson's list is still owed to you, and it is the sibling one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{برادر}} — \emph{barâdar} — \textbf{brother}
\end{quote}

Five letters, all already yours: \textbf{\fa{ب} \fa{ر} \fa{ا} \fa{د} \fa{ر}} — \emph{b}, \emph{r}, long \emph{â}, \emph{d}, \emph{r} again. Notice \textbf{\fa{ر}} opens and closes the word.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{برادر}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{brād(ar)}, from Indo-European *\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr} — the direct cousin of English \textbf{brother}, German \emph{Bruder}, and Latin \emph{frāter} (giving English \textbf{fraternal}). Unlike some kinship cousins, whose meanings narrow or shift as they travel, \textbf{brother} has meant exactly the same thing in every branch that kept it, for as long as anyone can trace it: this is as clean an inheritance as the family survives with.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{barâdar} — brother
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{barâdar} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr} $\to$ English \textbf{brother}, Latin \textbf{frāter}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{mâdar, pedar, barâdar} — mother, father, brother
  \item \emph{Name:} the one word the \textbf{\fa{بودن}} lesson still owes you
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\fa{برادر}} mean? (\textbf{Brother.}) Which English word is it the direct cousin of? (\textbf{Brother}.) Which family word from the \textbf{\fa{بودن}} lesson's list is still owed? (\textbf{\fa{دختر}}, daughter.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%A8\%D8\%B1\%D8\%A7\%D8\%AF\%D8\%B1}{Wiktionary: \fa{برادر}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dokhtar]{\fa{دختر} — daughter, and the family the \fa{بودن} lesson promised is complete}

\label{lesson:FA-C10-dokhtar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\fa{برادر}}. Then read \textbf{\fa{اسمِ} \fa{من} ... \fa{است}} once more, from the right edge — the very first sentence this track ever built, and the pattern this lesson reuses to close a family.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{دختر}} — \emph{dokhtar} — \textbf{daughter}
\end{quote}

Four letters, all already yours: \textbf{\fa{د} \fa{خ} \fa{ت} \fa{ر}} — \emph{d}, \textbf{kh}, \emph{t}, \emph{r}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: naming a family member as your own}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{دخترِ} \fa{من}} — \emph{dokhtar-e man} — \textbf{my daughter}
\end{quote}

The same ezafe \textbf{-e} from \textbf{\fa{اسمِ} \fa{من}} and \textbf{\fa{کلیدِ} \fa{من}} links a family word to its owner exactly the way it linked a name and a request. One grammar habit, three completely different kinds of noun.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{دختر}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{duxtar}, from Indo-European *\emph{d\textsuperscript{h}ugh\textsubscript{2}t\'{\={e}}r} — the direct cousin of English \textbf{daughter} and German \emph{Tochter}. An earlier lesson named four inherited family cousins in passing — \textbf{\fa{مادر}}, \textbf{\fa{پدر}}, \textbf{\fa{برادر}}, \textbf{\fa{دختر}} — while it was really teaching \textbf{\fa{بودن}}. This chapter and the last have now taught all four as full lessons: a promise made early, kept three chapters later.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{dokhtar} — daughter; then \textbf{dokhtar-e man} — my daughter
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{dokhtar} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{d\textsuperscript{h}ugh\textsubscript{2}tēr} $\to$ English \textbf{daughter}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{mâdar, pedar, barâdar, dokhtar} — all four, from memory
  \item \emph{Retrieve:} \textbf{\fa{اسمِ} \fa{من} ... \fa{است}}, the first sentence this track built, and its ezafe
  \item \emph{Name:} which of the four family words is the odd one out in sound — \textbf{\fa{دختر}}'s \textbf{kh}, where the other three have none
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name all four family words this chapter and the last have taught, in order. (\textbf{Mâdar, pedar, barâdar, dokhtar.}) Say “my daughter.” (\textbf{Dokhtar-e man.}) Which earlier sentence used the same ezafe? (\textbf{\fa{اسمِ} \fa{من} ... \fa{است}}, the very first sentence this track built.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AF\%D8\%AE\%D8\%AA\%D8\%B1}{Wiktionary: \fa{دختر}}.
